newsitem.title: CZECH REPUBLIC: TENNIS-PAST GREATS SET TO REKINDLE OLD RIVALRIES.
newsitem.headline: TENNIS-PAST GREATS SET TO REKINDLE OLD RIVALRIES.

text.p: Some of tennis's greatest figures are set to renew old rivalries as the ATP European Seniors' tour kicks off this weekend, looking to capitalise on some of the sport's most recognised personalities.

Bjorn Borg, Guillermo Vilas, and Andres Gomez -- with a total of 17 major titles between them -- head the list of Grand Slam champions scheduled to take the court from Thursday in Prague, part of the tour's six tournament schedule.

Despite last minute scratches by Jimmy Connors and Yannick Noah due to injury, ATP officials said they were hoping the personalities of the past, sadly lacking from the regular tour in recent years, would win back fans and bring the sport to more countries.

"This is the thing of the future. I am excited to be surrounded by the champions that I battled for years, to renew this is great," said Argentine Vilas, his trademark curly hair flowing as freely as his heavy topspin forehand.

Added former Czech Davis Cup captain Tomas Smid: "People now are missing the personalities like there were before. I think that is why people will come out, to see the players and refresh memories from a time when there were personalities on the court."

The ATP men's tour has faced criticism in recent months as being too boring, with rallies lasting no more than three or four hits as serves consistently travel over 200 kph and players more worried about endorsement contracts than having fun.

With an eye on the booming popularity of the PGA Senior's golf tour, ATP officials are anxious to showcase players that were household names in the 70s and 80s and hark back to a time when the actual playing time of a match was longer than the breaks in between games.
"The PGA tour in the U.S. is a perfect example even though we hope to have the tour worldwide which the PGA senior don't even have," tour official Edwin Weindorfer told Reuters.
Organisers know that with the likes of Borg, McEnroe, Connors and Ilie Nastase committed to playing in the tour, they have the prestige names needed to generate interest.
Nonetheless, they are taking no chances, teaming up with management group IMG to give the tour the marketing expertise, and possibly an extra hand in ensuring some players are motivated to play.
"It all depends on the first year. In tennis, you must have the top players and they must be involved a lot in other activities. If we do this, I think this has a big chance," Weindorfer said.
Though prize money pales in comparison to regular ATP tournaments -- total purses are set at $125,000 -- points will be awarded and rankings established with an eye on the tour growing.
"We have a lot of interest from markets that we are not currently in such as Spain, so we are trying to add tournaments and maybe next year we can expand to eight or nine events," Weindorfer said.

But the question remains to be seen whether players who once raced around the courts of Wimbledon, Roland Garros and for some Forest Hills, before the U.S. Open moved to Flushing Meadows, can still play exciting tennis.
"Everybody has something new in their game," said former French Open winner Gomez of Ecuador "We are slower, maybe a little, but the new equipment helps and we are changing with the game."
